name: Lena Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Lena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior lineworker at the Ferris Plains depot, out on the prairie, where it's wheat in every direction and the lines run straight for miles. I lead a crew of four, and we do new connections for grain dryers and irrigation pumps, pole changes, and in summer a lot of repairs after hail and lightning. In winter it's wind and ice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm good at it, and I like figuring out better ways to do things. I use an AI assistant every day to plan the week's jobs, check material lists and look up code changes, and I built a little calculator with it that tells farmers what a new connection will cost them. What wears me out is the low pay compared with the city crews, and how slow head office is to try anything new.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My boyfriend Mateo. He farms with his dad, about four hundred hectares of wheat and canola. We live in the old farmhouse on his family's land. I've got almost nothing saved because I bought a used pickup last year and paid for an online drone and robotics course out of my own pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got overhyped, and that's fine. I'd keep using it, because it saves me hours a week. At church, people would probably say they never trusted it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little bored, to be honest. I like new things and I'd hoped for more. But my job's secure, and I'd keep making the most of the tools I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal, keep using AI for planning and quotes. I'd try to sell my connection calculator idea to head office, or maybe to the other rural depots. And I'd start saving, maybe a hundred a month now the pickup's nearly paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about that online course. Why pay for it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the company wasn't going to, and I wanted to be ready. I did it in the evenings over three months. Mateo thought I was mad, sitting in the kitchen with a headset watching videos about drone flight rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone else at the depot use AI the way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Gus, the depot manager, calls it my little robot friend. But he's started asking me to run his reports through it, so he's coming round.

S0.say: I'd say it was a useful tool that got overhyped, and that's fine. I'd keep using it, because it saves me hours a week.
S0.think: I'd be a little bored, because I like new things and had hoped for more. But my job's secure and I'd keep making the most of the tools I've got.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for planning and quotes and tries to sell her connection cost calculator to head office or other rural depots. Starts saving about a hundred a month once her pickup is nearly paid off.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of restlessness.
S0.quote: Gus, the depot manager, calls it my little robot friend. But he's started asking me to run his reports through it, so he's coming round.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is a self-starter who paid for her own drone and robotics course and uses AI daily. Her savings are thin because of a pickup and that course. A plateau leaves her restless rather than relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. I'd tell the young ones at church youth group to get good at something real and learn the tools that go with it. I wouldn't want the government stepping in too much, just let people adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well here. I'm already trained on drones, I use AI every day, and I know the prairie lines better than anyone. If anything I'd worry that head office is too slow and some city contractor gets the work instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Gus and offer to run a drone inspection trial for the depot. On the side, I'd start offering drone inspections of farm wiring and grain bin connections to farmers around Ferris Plains, maybe a few hundred a job. I'd also look into what it would take to set up as a small contractor one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. This is my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, maybe, because he's fifty-eight and doesn't want to learn anything new. And Mateo's dad, if farms get more automated and he can't keep up. But they're both stubborn, and stubborn people usually find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from to get the side business going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already have the drone, a second-hand one I bought with my tax refund. I'd keep costs low, use the pickup, and reinvest every job back in. I wouldn't borrow unless I had to.

S1.say: This is a chance for people willing to work and learn, so get good at something real and learn the tools that go with it. I wouldn't want the government stepping in too much.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, being trained on drones, using AI daily and knowing the prairie lines better than anyone. I'd worry more that head office is too slow and a city contractor takes the work.
S1.do: Offers to run a drone inspection trial for her depot and starts doing paid drone inspections of farm wiring on the side. Looks into what it would take to set up as a small contractor, reinvesting every job's earnings.
S1.feel: Calm and actually excited, because this is her kind of change.
S1.quote: But they're both stubborn, and stubborn people usually find a way.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as an opportunity and would move first, both at work and with a side business. Her free-market outlook shows in wanting the government to stay out of the way. Her main worry is her own company being too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, but people and families can handle it if they're given room to build new things. I'd say the government should help with loans and training, not just send everyone a cheque. Most people I know would rather work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be nervous. I'd be ready on the skills side, but two years means big companies with deep pockets get the robots first, and I'd have nothing saved to compete. Mateo's farm might be okay, but even that's not certain if robots do farming too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go to Gus and push to be the depot's robot crew lead, and if head office said no, I'd look at starting a small contracting firm to run robot inspections and repairs for the rural co-ops. I'd apply for a small business loan and maybe ask Mateo's dad to co-sign. I'd keep my job until the firm had enough work to pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see what to do, but it's a big risk with no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo if you were taking out a loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, this is the bet, and if it fails, we'll live on the farm and I'll find something else. He'd probably say go for it, then lie awake worrying. That's how it goes with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build up savings and a name. With two years, I'm racing companies that already have money. I think I could still do it, but it'd be close.

S2.say: This is a shock, but people and families can handle it if they're given room to build new things. The government should help with loans and training, not just send everyone a cheque.
S2.think: I'd be nervous, because I'm ready on skills but big companies would get the robots first and I'd have nothing saved to compete. Mateo's farm might be okay, but even that's not certain.
S2.do: Pushes to become her depot's robot crew lead in the first months and, if refused, starts a small contracting firm for rural co-ops. Applies for a business loan with her partner's father as possible co-signer, keeping her job until the firm pays.
S2.feel: Anxious, because she can see what to do but it's a big risk with no cushion.
S2.quote: I'd tell him straight, this is the bet, and if it fails, we'll live on the farm and I'll find something else.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario she wants to build rather than wait, though thin savings make it a real gamble. She'd lean on family for a co-signer, not the state. Her fallback is the farm, which gives her some security others lack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone who's willing to adapt. I'd be telling people to learn now. And I'd say small local businesses should get a chance, not just the big players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I like this one. Five years gives me time to save, get the side business established, and move into robot work properly before everyone else. I'd be thirty-two and I could have my own small firm by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd grow the drone inspection work on weekends and save every dollar from it, aiming for six months of business costs by year two. I'd keep pushing head office to try robot equipment at Ferris Plains, with me leading. By year three I'd register a company and buy my first piece of robot equipment, probably second-hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big job that I know I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by year three. What would that first piece of equipment be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a line-inspection robot, the kind that crawls along the conductor and checks for damage. I've watched videos of them. One of those plus my drone and I could cover a whole county of farm lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a gamble. Five is a plan with a bit of risk in it. I like plans with a bit of risk.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for anyone willing to adapt, so learn now. Small local businesses should get a chance, not just the big players.
S3.think: I like this one, because five years gives me time to save, establish the side business and move into robot work before everyone else. At thirty-two I could have my own small firm.
S3.do: Grows weekend drone inspection work and saves it all, aiming for six months of business costs by year two. Pushes head office to trial robot equipment at her depot and plans to register a company and buy second-hand robot equipment by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like before a big job she knows she can do.
S3.quote: One of those plus my drone and I could cover a whole county of farm lines.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from a gamble into a business she can build carefully. She has a specific piece of equipment in mind, a robot that crawls along conductors. Her outlook links hard work, small business and staying in her community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd tell people to start a business, learn a trade, and plan. At church I'd say we should look after the families who struggle with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out well. I'd be thirty-seven with a small contracting firm running robot crews for rural co-ops, and maybe a few employees. Mateo's farm would probably be automated too, and we'd manage it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd keep doing my job and keep learning, and build the side business slowly, with no loans. I'd save, and in three or four years I'd buy robot equipment and start hiring. Mateo and I would get married in the next couple of years, because I wouldn't want to wait for all this to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the future I'd actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in this version still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, and people like him. If he doesn't want to learn, he'll be left behind, and I'd feel bad about that. I'd probably offer him a job, honestly, doing what he's best at, which is knowing every farmer by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with the other two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm gambling. Five, I'm building fast. Ten, I'm building properly, and I get to keep the life I want out here.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for not getting ready: start a business, learn a trade and plan. At church I'd say we should look after the families who struggle with it.
S4.think: I think I'd come out well, at thirty-seven with a small firm running robot crews for rural co-ops and a few employees. Mateo's farm would probably be automated too, and we'd manage it together.
S4.do: Keeps her job, keeps learning and builds the side business slowly without loans. Buys robot equipment and starts hiring in three or four years, and plans to marry her partner within the next couple of years.
S4.feel: Calm, as if this is the future she actually wants.
S4.quote: I'd probably offer him a job, honestly, doing what he's best at, which is knowing every farmer by name.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's confident and clearly enjoys picturing her own firm. Her care for people like Gus shows a community side to her free-market views. She'd go ahead with marriage without waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have the skills but no savings, and the big companies would get there first. What would help is small business loans and grants for local firms, and rules that give rural contractors a fair shot at the work, not just the big city outfits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me want to own the future or just survive it. Out here, if you don't build your own thing, somebody from the city will build it for you and take the profit home.

headlineQuote: Out here, if you don't build your own thing, somebody from the city will build it for you and take the profit home.
portrait: Lena Reyes is a 27-year-old senior lineworker on the prairie who uses AI every day, built a cost calculator for farmers and paid for her own drone and robotics course. She lives with her boyfriend Mateo on his family's farm and has almost nothing saved after buying a pickup. The slow scenarios leave her calm and even excited, and the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because she'd have the skills but no cushion to compete. With five or ten years she plans to build her own contracting firm running robot crews for rural co-ops, believing in hard work, family and small local business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have the skills but no savings, and big companies would get there first.
whatWouldHelp: Small business loans and grants for local firms, and rules that give rural contractors a fair shot at the work.
